name: Ozumacín Chinantec
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Rupp, James (2017) Propuesta de convenciones para escribir el chinanteco de Ozumacin, ILV Mexico (cited on Wikipedia; sil.org returns 403)

new_statements.quote: El prefijo läˉ- se combina con un adjetivo y lo convierte en un verbo intransitivo. Es posible que el verbo laꜗ ser, suceder sea la fuente de este prefijo. Puesto que el acento básico de la palabra siempre aparece en la última sílaba, la vocal del prefijo está en una posición que no se acentúa, lo que permite que la pronunciación de la vocal a se "afloje", es decir, se pronuncie como la vocal ä.
new_statements.translation: The prefix läˉ- combines with an adjective and turns it into an intransitive verb. It is possible that the verb laꜗ 'to be, to happen' is the source of this prefix. Since the basic accent of the word always appears on the last syllable, the vowel of the prefix is in a position that is not accented, which allows the pronunciation of the vowel a to 'loosen', that is, to be pronounced as the vowel ä.
new_statements.citation: Rupp, James E. (comp.). 2012. Diccionario chinanteco para Ayotzintepec, Ozumacín y Progreso. Primera edición. México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano, A.C. xx+274 pp. Gramática chinanteca, sec. 5.1 'Derivación por medio de prefijos'.
new_statements.locator: Gramática chinanteca sec. 5.1, printed p. 254 = PDF p. 275 (text-layer lines 12364-12369 of); tone/ballistic-accent description on printed pp. xi-xii = PDF pp. 12-13
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (the 'acento básico de la palabra') always falls on the final syllable, which is the root/stem syllable; the tense, directional and derivational prefixes (miˉ-, läˉ-, dsaˉ-, yaˉ-, llaˉ-, maˉ-, gaꜙ- etc.) that precede it are unstressed, and their vowels reduce (a > ä). The 'acento' described in the front matter is a different thing: a contrastive ballistic accent (rapid pitch fall) that can co-occur with each of the three level tones on any syllable and is written with a dot on the tone mark.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated ('siempre'). The statement is made in passing in the derivational-morphology section, not in a phonology chapter; the dictionary's own phonological front matter (pp. ix-xii) treats only consonants, vowels, nine tones and tone sandhi.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the morphological word (prefix(es) + monosyllabic root, with optional person suffix fused into the root syllable); the example is the derived verb dsaˉläˉlle̱ey̱ꜘ 'to get angry'. Tone sandhi before pause (p. xii) is phrase-level and separate from stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary covers the single variety spoken in San Pedro Ozumacín, Ayotzintepec (dialect centre per Rupp 1987) and Santiago Progreso = ISO chz = ozum1235; no sub-variety is singled out and there is no separate glottocode for Ayotzintepec. Rupp 1987 notes the closest language is Palantla Chinantec (63% intelligibility).

Puesto que el acento básico de la palabra siempre aparece en la última sílaba, la vocal del prefijo está en una posición que no se acentúa, lo que permite que la pronunciación de la vocal a se "afloje", es decir, se pronuncie como la vocal ä.
sources.locator: Gramática chinanteca sec. 5.1, printed p. 254 = PDF p. 275 (text-layer lines 12364-12369 of); tone/ballistic-accent description on printed pp. xi-xii = PDF pp. 12-13
sources.note: Front matter pp. ix-xii describes consonants, vowels, three level tones, the same tones 'con acento' (ballistic accent: pitch falls rapidly, written with a dot on the tone mark) and three rising tones, plus tone sandhi; 'acento' there means ballistic accent, not word stress. The only word-stress statement is incidental, in grammar sec. 5.1 (printed p. 254, PDF p. 275): the basic accent of the word always falls on the last syllable, so a prefix vowel is in an unaccented position and laxes (a -> ä). Verified against the page image.

sources.citation: Rupp, James E. & Nadine Rupp. 1996. Diccionario chinanteco de San Juan Lealao, Oaxaca (VIMSA 35), grammar sketch sec. 0.4-0.5, p. 388 (already held under leal1235, scanned).
sources.note: Mentions Ozumacín only to compare diphthongs after velars (chiah? 'chachalaca' = Ozumacín [kia??]); its 'acento balístico' section concerns Lealao, not Ozumacín.

sources.citation: Rupp, James E. 2017. Propuesta de convenciones para escribir el chinanteco de Ozumacín. (Propuestas de convenciones para escribir las lenguas originarias de México 4.) México: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano, A.C. 9 pp. SIL Mexico archive entry 69123.
sources.note: Sec. 3 'Tonos' (p. 5): Chinantec languages are tonal; every syllable carries a written tone; marks differ when a 'ballistic' accent falls on the syllable (realized as a rapid fall in pitch); nine tones listed. App. B (p. 8): IPA consonant/vowel inventory, ten vowel qualities, nine tones. No statement about word stress.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Ozumacín Chinantec' (English; phonology section sourced to Rupp 2017), read 2026-09-17.
sources.note: Vowels, consonants, nine tones, 'Ballistic syllables are marked by a steep drop in pitch'; nothing on word stress.

sources.citation: SIL Mexico language page 'Chinanteco de Ozumacín' (James and Nadine Rupp) and SIL archive records 53130, 69123, 10699, 4391, 10889; Wayback 2015 listing of sil.org/resources/search/language/chz (8 items).
sources.note: No linguistic statement on stress; notes ten vowels (monophthongised diphthongs) and absence of whistle speech. Lists all SIL holdings for chz: dictionary 2012, propuesta 2017, animacy 2009, texts 1994, Workpapers 1987, Krotzer 1970 Tlalocan text, three 1985 primers.

sources.citation: Priest, Lorna A. 2004. Revised proposal to encode Chinantec tone marks. Unicode L2/04-349R. 5 pp.
sources.note: Only inventories the Ozumacín tone/ballistic-accent orthographic marks (citing the 1990 Mark and 2003 NT); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Rupp, James E. 1987. The multipurpose Chinantec word ja̱³. SIL-Mexico Workpapers 9: 122-128. (full scan, no text layer; plus Rosetta Project scanned excerpts of p. 122, language detail and bibliography). SIL Mexico archive entry 10889.
sources.note: Phoneme note on p. 122 (read from page image): consonants, ten vowels (oral/nasal, short/long), three tone levels 1-3, 'The level tones may also occur with a ballistic accent, which is symbolized with an apostrophe after the tone number', and three tone glides. Nothing on word stress. Detail note: Ayotzintepec is the centre of the dialect; closest language Palantla Chinantec (63% intelligibility).
